title: Corner of Blood
text:
So small, the sweet marjoram,

and... how it smells!

So small.


At night, beneath the morning star,

so small, the sweet marjoram,

and how it smells!


And... when it rains in the afternoon,

how it smells!


And when the sun rises,

so small, the sweet marjoram,

how it smells!


And now, as I live from dream,

how it smells,

so small, the sweet marjoram!


How it hurts!...

so small, the sweet marjoram.

So small.
editorial_note: The translation renders 'almoraduj' as sweet marjoram and keeps the refrain's turn from scent to pain.

title: Come, Put Your Hand Into Me
text:
...



through the deep dark vein of my flesh.

Inside, your arm will curdle

        with my shadow;

it will become night-stone,

dry root of

        blood...


The fountain of my chest coagulated,

to ask for help

it will rise

        to my throat.


Deny it if it is life!

Drive your arm deeper into me!...

        Cross me with it!


Pierce me!

Though it cost me the tree of my body,

        lead me to you, death.
editorial_note: The source is fragmentary at the opening; the translation preserves the ellipsis and the bodily death-invocation.

title: Come, Put Your Hand Into Me...
text:
Come, put your hand into me...

        Come, put your hand into me


through the deep dark vein of my flesh.

Inside, your arm will curdle

        with my shadow;

it will become night-stone,

dry root of

        blood...


The fountain of my chest coagulated,

to ask for help

it will rise

        to my throat.


Deny it if it is life!

Drive your arm deeper into me!...

        Cross me with it!


Pierce me!

Though it cost me the tree of my body,

        lead me to you, death.
editorial_note: The catalog title differs, but the visible body begins 'Come, put your hand into me'; this entry preserves that body.

title: Mary Stuart
text:
Pale the color, on the white brow

a furrow that reveals grief,

the blue pupil directed toward heaven,

the firm step, the prudent gesture,


ardent weeping bathes her beautiful face.

Sleeplessness is marked on her countenance,

and a dress of black velvet

richly imprisons her forms.


Thus Mary Stuart walks slowly,

her modest breast shattered,

to the gloomy and bloody scaffold;


and as her head rolled on the platform,

there rolled on the ground, to eternal shame,

the dishonored name of her cousin.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the historical tableau and the final blame cast toward Mary Stuart's cousin.

title: Sad Song
text:
I did not want,

I did not want to have been born.


I sat beside the fountain,

looking at the new afternoon...


The water sprang up, slowly.

I did not want to have been born.


I went beneath the poplar grove

to hide in its sadness.


The wind was weeping in it.

I did not want to have been born.


I leaned against a stone,

to see the first star...


Beautiful summer tear!

I did not want to have been born.


I slept beneath the moon.

What fine knife-light!


I rose from my sorrow...


(I was already sunk in dream.)


I did not want,

I did not want to have been born.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated refrain and the delicate natural images around despair.
